The attack — the latest of several in the past week on King Khalid International Airport — is expected to increase Saudi pressure on allies including the United States to provide military support for the kingdom.

items.title: Trump Says U.S. May Join Saudi Strikes on Houthis After Riyadh Airport Attacks
items.standfirst: Attacks on Saudi airports have killed several people and disrupted hundreds of flights, prompting Washington to consider a larger military role in Yemen.
items.content: U.S. President Donald Trump told members of the media that "we may" join Saudi strikes against the Houthis during a press meet on the White House South Lawn on Oct. 10, 2026, in Washington, D.C. —Aaron Schwartz—Getty ImagesPresident Donald Trump said Saturday that the United States “may” join Saudi Arabia’s strikes on the Iran-backed Houthi militia group, which is based in Yemen, after airport attacks killed at least 18 people in recent days. The latest attack led to near-complete shutdown of public air traffic into and out of the capital.“We may. We’re going to look at it,” Trump told reporters on the South Lawn of the White House, prior to departing for a rally in Tennessee. “We just found out about the recent attack. So we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly.”His comments came shortly after a fresh attack on Saturday, in which a missile struck the complex housing Terminals 3 and 4 of King Khalid International Airport (KKIA), the second-busiest airport in Saudi Arabia. Twelve people were killed and over 300 were injured, according to the General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA). The Houthis, who claimed attacks on the airport earlier in the week, did not immediately claim the latest strike.It was the latest in a series of attacks over the past week, which began just days after Yemen’s Saudi-backed government announced a major offensive against the Houthis on Oct. 4. Read More: Houthi Attacks on Saudi Airports Kill 3 Amid Escalating War in YemenTwo took place on Tuesday and Wednesday, although the information about each has been scarce. A strike on the more southerly Abha International Airport killed two women—one Algerian and one Moroccan—while an attack on KKIA left one Sudanese man dead, the country’s civil aviation authorities said on Wednesday. The Houthis said they again targeted KKIA on Thursday; three Saudi citizens, including a pilot, died. The victims of the past week’s strikes were primarily Saudi but also included individuals from Algeria, Bangladesh, Egypt, Jordan, Morocco, Pakistan, the Philippines, Sudan, and the United States.Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki, a spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen, said in a statement on Friday that the attacks “will not go unpunished.” —Elif Acar—Anadolu via Getty ImagesAirport strikes are a signature strategy from the Houthis; a similar move on Abha in 2019 was denounced as an apparent war crime by the Human Rights Watch. Brigadier General Yahya Saree, a Houthi military spokesperson, on Thursday reiterated an earlier warning for international airlines and passengers to avoid airspace over Saudi Arabia, which had on Monday been declared an open military operations zone. He also warned employees to avoid Saudi oil facilities so as not to endanger their lives, since they are considered primary targets. The GACA announced that Riyadh had suspended operations at its main airport on Saturday and was assessing the damage; FlightAware showed 400 cancellations into and out of KKIA as of 11 p.m. local time.The U.S. Embassy in Riyadh also issued a security alert, warning Americans to avoid KKIA and its surrounding areas as of Saturday. “U.S. citizens should be aware of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions. We recommend checking your flight departure status directly with the airline and with the airport,” its website said.Why has the Saudi-Houthi conflict escalated?The latest airport attacks followed months of escalating threats to air travel and shipping. In July, the Houthis accused the Saudis of bombing Sanaa International Airport. Yemen’s Saudi-backed government claimed responsibility, saying it had sought to prevent an Iranian plane from landing there. In response, the Houthis said that they would impose a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia. The Houthis last month captured both the port city of Mokha and Perim Island in a bid to control the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. With shipping through the Strait of Hormuz already disrupted by the U.S. war with Iran, a threat to traffic through Bab el-Mandeb could deepen the global oil crisis.In the weeks to follow, Saudi-backed forces have since claimed to retake both seized areas, but the claim has not been independently verified and control remains disputed.In September, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman urged Trump to act against the Houthis. The request came as the militia group gained ground over vital chokepoints in the Red Sea. Although the two nations are allies, Washington explained last month that it did not have plans to get involved in the conflict. TIME has reached out to the White House for comment as the situation evolves.Trump’s renewed consideration of strikes in Yemen comes as the war with Iran remains deeply unpopular at home: 69% of Americans said it had not been worth fighting in an AP-NORC poll from Oct. 1. On Thursday, Trump said the U.S. would not attack Iran before the Nov. 3 midterms—a pledge that does not address possible strikes on the Houthis in Yemen.
